title: 9/11’s shrinking shadow
gist: Twenty-five years on, the author argues 9/11's claim to being a historical pivot rests less on the attack itself than on the millennial 'end of history' complacency it shattered and the disproportionate US reaction that followed — while a younger cohort increasingly ranks China's rise, the GFC, Covid, warming and AI adoption as more consequential.

insights.claim: A growing discourse, mostly among people born after or too young to remember 9/11, questions why the attack is still treated as exceptional pivot point in world history.
insights.so_what: Foundational security narratives decay generationally; the political constituency for counterterrorism budgets and War-on-Terror framing erodes as the cohort that lived it ages out.
insights.quote: An event 25 years ago that felt world-ending to the people who lived through it, but is now considered just another chapter in the history books.
insights.speaker: Lydia Khalil

insights.claim: The competing candidates for the quarter-century's most consequential events are the rise of China, the global financial crisis, the Covid pandemic, global warming and the mass adoption of artificial intelligence.
insights.so_what: A useful ranking of the structural drivers a long-horizon allocator should weight above terrorism risk.
insights.speaker: Lydia Khalil

themes.theme: Context, not casualties, made the event singular

insights.claim: 9/11's impact derives from its context — arriving after the peaceful 1990s interlude when 'end of history' complacency was widely believed — rather than from the attack's scale alone.
insights.so_what: Shock magnitude is a function of prior consensus complacency, a reusable lens for pricing tail events into markets that believe risk has been abolished.
insights.quote: we had reached the “end of history”
insights.locator: It was the turn of the millennium
insights.speaker: Lydia Khalil

insights.claim: What embossed 9/11 as distinct was the furious US reaction that followed — the author's image of a giant Gulliver roused from slumber and lashing out — as much as the attack itself.
insights.so_what: The second-order policy overreaction, not the initial event, produced the lasting geopolitical and fiscal consequences — a pattern worth watching after any future shock.
insights.quote: a giant Gulliver roused from slumber and lashing out
insights.locator: It is this context, and the furious reaction
insights.speaker: Lydia Khalil

insights.claim: Expert opinion canvassed at the 20th anniversary split between those arguing the attacks and War on Terror reordered global politics and those contending the strategic effects were contained and eclipsed by China's rise, technological disruption and environmental impacts.
insights.so_what: Even specialists cannot agree the event changed the trajectory — a caution against anchoring long-run scenarios on single dramatic shocks.
insights.locator: I put the question then to six experts
insights.speaker: Lydia Khalil

insights.claim: With the Taliban back in Kabul and the terrorism threat now more fragmented and diffuse, the strategic returns on the entire post-9/11 campaign are open to question.
insights.so_what: A diffuse, fragmented threat profile argues for distributed domestic resilience spending rather than expeditionary military budgets.
insights.locator: Now, with the Taliban back in Kabul
insights.speaker: Lydia Khalil
